stem: After enabling prompt caching on a 40,000-token league rulebook, a finance analyst sees input_tokens drop to a few hundred per request and concludes the requests now process far less content. The dashboard only sums input_tokens. Which correction best fits?

options.text: The analyst is right: caching compresses the rulebook, so far fewer tokens get processed now.
options.explanation: Caching doesn't compress anything. The full rulebook is still processed from the cache.

options.text: Cached tokens are free, so input_tokens is now the only input that is billed at all.
options.explanation: Cache reads and cache writes are billed, at their own multipliers of the input price.

options.text: Total input is input_tokens plus cache_creation_input_tokens plus cache_read_input_tokens.
options.explanation: Correct. With caching, input_tokens covers only the uncached part after the last breakpoint. The dashboard must add all three fields.

options.text: The rulebook now sits in the cache instead of the context window, so it no longer counts.
options.explanation: Cached tokens still occupy the context window. Caching changes price and latency, not size.

stem: A scouting assistant sends a 15,000-token stable instruction block followed by a different scout question on each request. The developer put the cache_control breakpoint on the question block, and logs show a cache write on every request but no reads. Which change best fits?

options.text: Move the breakpoint to the end of the stable instruction block, before the varying question.
options.explanation: Correct. A breakpoint after the varying question makes each request's prefix unique, so every request writes and none read. Putting it at the end of the shared part lets every request read it.

options.text: Add breakpoints on both the instructions and the question, so either one can be read.
options.explanation: The question block changes every time, so its breakpoint only adds writes. The fix is the shared-prefix breakpoint.

options.text: Switch to the 1-hour cache duration so the question block stays cached for longer.
options.explanation: Duration doesn't help when each prefix is unique. A different question never matches an earlier write.

options.text: Shorten the instruction block below the minimum cacheable length to avoid write costs.
options.explanation: This disables caching entirely and pays full price for the instructions on every request.

stem: A coaching chatbot holds conversations that run to 40 or more turns. The developer placed a single cache breakpoint on the first user message, so later turns read only the system prompt and first message from cache. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Remove the breakpoint and resend the full conversation uncached on each and every turn.
options.explanation: This pays full input price for the entire growing history on every turn.

options.text: Place one breakpoint on every message in the conversation to cache each turn.
options.explanation: There are at most four breakpoints per request, and marking every message isn't needed.

options.text: Start a fresh conversation every ten turns so the cached prefix stays short.
options.explanation: Resetting throws away context the user expects Claude to keep, and still pays full price for each reset.

options.text: Put the breakpoint on the latest turn and move it forward with each new request.
options.explanation: Correct. Moving the checkpoint forward lets each request read the whole prior conversation from cache and write only the new part. Automatic caching does this for you.

stem: A nightly Message Batches job sends 2,000 scouting-report requests that share a 30,000-token league context, followed by a per-player section. The batch can take more than an hour to finish, and cache reads are rarer than expected. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Disable caching for the batch, because the batch discount and cache discounts can't be combined.
options.explanation: The discounts stack. Caching and batch pricing can apply to the same request.

options.text: Mark the shared context with a 1-hour cache duration so it survives the gaps between requests.
options.explanation: Correct. Batch requests run concurrently and in any order over a long window, so cache hits are best-effort. The 1-hour duration keeps the shared context available across those gaps.

options.text: Keep the 5-minute duration, because every cache read refreshes the entry and keeps it alive.
options.explanation: Reads do refresh the entry, but with requests spread unevenly over hours, gaps longer than five minutes let it expire.

options.text: Move the per-player section ahead of the shared context so the batch writes fewer caches.
options.explanation: Putting varying content first makes every prefix unique, which removes the cache benefit entirely.

stem: A team generates detailed scouting notes for every college prospect each night; nobody reads them until morning. Every request repeats the same 20,000-token evaluation rubric, and the bill has doubled. Which two changes reduce cost without lowering quality? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Set max_tokens well below the typical note length to cap output spend.
options.explanation: Truncated notes have to be regenerated, so the retries cost more and quality drops.

options.text: Send the nightly requests through the Message Batches API.
options.explanation: Correct. Work nobody waits for fits the Batch API, which costs half the standard price for input and output.

options.text: Turn on fast mode so each note finishes sooner and uses less time.
options.explanation: Fast mode costs more per token. It buys speed, not savings.

options.text: Stop logging usage fields, since logging adds to the request size.
options.explanation: Usage fields come back in the response and cost nothing. Without them you can't see where money goes.

options.text: Cache the shared rubric so later requests read it at a discount.
options.explanation: Correct. A large prefix repeated in every request is the classic caching case, and cache discounts stack with batch pricing.

stem: Product wants a monthly cost forecast for a new trade-analysis feature before launch. A spreadsheet multiplies the average prompt's word count by the input price and the average visible answer length by the output price. Which approach gives the most reliable forecast?

options.text: Keep the spreadsheet but use the median request size, since outliers distort averages.
options.explanation: The expensive tail matters for budgets. Ignoring it understates cost, and the word-based inputs are still guesses.

options.text: Use the context window size as the per-request input, assuming every request fills it.
options.explanation: This wildly overstates input and says nothing about output, which costs more per token.

options.text: Run real sample requests, log usage with thinking, and model cost per completed task.
options.explanation: Correct. Real usage fields capture tokenizer effects and hidden thinking output. Costing whole tasks, retries and the tail included, gives a realistic forecast.

options.text: Count only visible answer text as output, since thinking tokens aren't shown to users.
options.explanation: Thinking is billed as output even when it isn't displayed, so this undercounts the most expensive tokens.

stem: When a new game file arrives, a highlights service immediately fires 50 parallel requests that share a 40,000-token cached prefix, each asking about a different quarter or player. Usage shows cache writes on almost every request and very few reads, though the prefix is identical. Which change best fits?

options.text: Send one request first, wait for its response to begin, then fan out the remaining requests.
options.explanation: Correct. A cache entry becomes available only after the first response begins. Requests sent at the same moment can't read an entry that doesn't exist yet, so warm the cache first.

options.text: Give each parallel request its own cache breakpoint location so they write to different entries.
options.explanation: Different breakpoints create more writes, not more reads. The problem is timing.

options.text: Switch the requests to the 1-hour cache duration so the entries are kept for longer.
options.explanation: Duration doesn't help when the entry doesn't exist yet. All 50 requests arrive before any write completes.

options.text: Raise the account's rate limit so all fifty requests are processed in a single batch.
options.explanation: Rate limits don't change cache timing, and more parallelism makes the simultaneous-write problem worse.

stem: Finance wants to see Claude spending broken down by app and by environment (development, staging, production) across six product teams, without asking each team for spreadsheets. Which two steps best fit? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use the Usage and Cost Admin API to report usage and cost by workspace, API key and model.
options.explanation: Correct. The Usage and Cost API reports usage and USD cost across the organization, broken down by dimensions such as workspace, API key and model. It needs an Admin API key.

options.text: Give every team the organization's Admin API key so each one can export its own numbers.
options.explanation: Admin keys carry organization-wide power. Spreading them widely is a security risk, and central reporting already covers the need.

options.text: Ask each team to put its team name in the system prompt so the bill can be searched later.
options.explanation: Prompt text doesn't appear in billing data. It only adds input tokens to every request.

options.text: Give each app and environment its own workspace or API key so costs can be attributed.
options.explanation: Correct. Separating workspaces or keys per app and environment makes the usage and cost breakdown map directly to owners.

options.text: Sum response.usage from each team's local logs once a quarter and estimate the rest.
options.explanation: Local logs are useful per app, but quarterly manual roll-ups are slow and incomplete for organization-wide attribution.

stem: A ticketing assistant caches its 12,000-token system prompt, but `cache_read_input_tokens` is zero on every request. The system prompt begins with the line `Current time: <timestamp>`, filled in per request so Claude knows the date. Which fix best fits?

options.text: Add three more `cache_control` breakpoints inside the system prompt so some part of it gets cached
options.explanation: The timestamp is at the very start, so every later breakpoint also sits after changed bytes. More breakpoints still produce no reads.

options.text: Move the timestamp out of the cached prefix, for example into the user message after the breakpoint
options.explanation: Correct. Caching is a prefix match, so any changing byte early in the prefix invalidates everything after it. Volatile content belongs after the last breakpoint.

options.text: Switch to the 1-hour cache TTL so entries survive long enough to be read
options.explanation: The entries never match in the first place. A longer TTL doesn't help a prefix that changes on every request.

options.text: Round the timestamp to the nearest second so consecutive requests are more likely to match
options.explanation: Requests seconds apart would still differ, so the prefix still changes almost every time.

stem: A team's cost model for a game-strategy assistant multiplied the length of the visible answers by the output price. The real bill is about three times the forecast. The app uses adaptive thinking, and thinking is not displayed to users. What best explains the gap, and what should change?

options.text: Hidden thinking is free, so the gap must come from input; trim the system prompt
options.explanation: Hiding thinking changes what is returned, not what is billed. The premise is wrong.

options.text: Output is billed per character, not per token; recompute the forecast by character count
options.explanation: Billing is per token. Switching to characters would make the model less accurate, not more.

options.text: The pricing page must be out of date; ask the vendor to correct the invoice
options.explanation: The invoice reflects real usage. The forecast left out a whole category of output tokens.

options.text: Thinking tokens are billed as output even when hidden; model from `usage.output_tokens` and tune effort
options.explanation: Correct. `output_tokens` includes thinking. Forecasting from logged usage captures it, and effort is the lever for how much the model spends.

stem: To cut costs on a weekly team-report generator, a developer lowers `max_tokens` from 8,000 to 1,000. Many reports now end mid-sentence, the pipeline retries them, and the total bill goes up. Which approach best fits the original goal?

options.text: Restore a safe `max_tokens`, then lower effort and tighten the output instructions
options.explanation: Correct. `max_tokens` is a hard cap, so setting it too low causes truncation and paid retries. Effort and instructions reduce spend without cutting answers off, and cost per completed report shows the real effect.

options.text: Keep the 1,000 cap and stitch truncated reports together across several follow-up requests
options.explanation: Each follow-up resends the context and adds turns, so this is likely to cost more than one complete answer.

options.text: Lower `max_tokens` further so truncated attempts waste fewer tokens before the retry
options.explanation: More truncation means more retries. The waste grows rather than shrinks.

options.text: Disable retries so truncated reports are delivered as they are
options.explanation: This lowers the bill by shipping broken reports, which doesn't meet the feature's purpose.

stem: A lightweight fan-trivia bot marks its 300-token system prompt with `cache_control`. Requests succeed with no errors, but `cache_creation_input_tokens` and `cache_read_input_tokens` are always zero. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Caching only works with the Message Batches API, not with real-time requests
options.explanation: Prompt caching works on ordinary Messages requests. The batch API is a separate cost lever.

options.text: The cache needs a warm-up period of about an hour before it starts serving reads
options.explanation: There is no warm-up period. A cacheable prefix is written on the first request and can be read on the next.

options.text: The prefix is below the model's minimum cacheable length, so it silently isn't cached
options.explanation: Correct. Prefixes shorter than the model-dependent minimum don't cache, and the API raises no error, so zero cache fields are the only sign.

options.text: `cache_control` is only accepted on user messages, so a system-prompt marker is ignored
options.explanation: System prompt blocks can carry `cache_control`; it is a common place to put a breakpoint.

stem: A nightly job sends 10,000 independent requests. Each has 2,000 input tokens and 500 output tokens. At list prices of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, and with the Message Batches API billing at 50% of standard prices, what does the job cost as a batch?

options.explanation: This applies the discount to input tokens only ($20 + $50). Batch pricing halves output tokens as well.
Correct. At standard prices, input is 20M tokens at $2/M ($40) and output is 5M tokens at $10/M ($50), so $90 in total. The batch discount halves every token, giving $45.
$90 is the standard (non-batch) price. The batch discount applies to the whole request.
This applies the discount to output tokens only ($40 + $25). Batch pricing halves input tokens as well.

stem: Ten requests share a 50,000-token prefix and all start within five minutes of each other. Base input costs $2 per million tokens. A 5-minute cache write costs 1.25× base, and a cache read costs 0.1× base. Ignoring the uncached tail of each request, what does the prefix cost across all ten requests with caching, compared with $1.00 without it?

options.text: About $0.22: one write (50k × $2.50/M = $0.125) plus nine reads (450k × $0.20/M = $0.09).
options.explanation: Correct. The first request pays the write premium, and the next nine read the prefix at a tenth of the base price.

options.text: $1.00: caching only reduces latency, not cost.
options.explanation: Cache reads are billed at a fraction of the base input price, so caching cuts cost substantially.

options.text: About $1.25: every request pays the write premium.
options.explanation: Only the first request writes. The later requests read the cache.

options.text: About $0.10: ten reads at $0.20 per million.
options.explanation: This forgets that the first request has to write the cache at 1.25× before any reads happen.

stem: A support chat caches a 30,000-token system prompt. Users typically reply about every 20 minutes, and each reply triggers a request. With the default 5-minute TTL, almost every request writes the cache again. Which choice best fits?

options.text: Use the 1-hour TTL. Its write costs 2× base instead of 1.25×, but the entry survives the 20-minute gaps, so later turns read from the cache instead of rewriting it.
options.explanation: Correct. The TTL should match the gap between requests that share a prefix. Gaps of 5–60 minutes are where the 1-hour TTL pays off.

options.text: Add more cache breakpoints so that some of the entries survive.
options.explanation: Every entry expires on the same timer. More breakpoints don't extend their lifetime.

options.text: Keep the 5-minute TTL, because it is always the cheaper option.
options.explanation: The 5-minute TTL is cheaper only when requests arrive less than five minutes apart. Here it expires between almost every pair of turns.

options.text: Turn caching off, since the cache keeps expiring anyway.
options.explanation: With the right TTL the cache would hit on most turns, and turning it off throws that saving away.

stem: After moving a support bot from an Opus-tier model to a Haiku-tier model, cost per request fell 70%. But escalations to human agents doubled, and the average number of turns per resolved conversation rose from 3 to 7. How should the team judge whether the switch saved money?

options.text: Compare only the token prices of the two models.
options.explanation: Unit prices say nothing about how many requests and escalations each completed task needs.

options.text: Use cost per request, because that's what the API bills.
options.explanation: Cost per request ignores the extra turns and escalations the switch caused.

options.text: Compare cost per resolved conversation, including the extra turns and the cost of human escalations, rather than cost per request.
options.explanation: Correct. What matters is the cost of a completed task. A cheaper request that needs more turns or human handling may cost more in total.

options.text: Count only the human-escalation cost, since the API spend went down.
options.explanation: Both components matter. The extra turns are API spend that needs to be counted too.

stem: A team must reduce Claude API spend without lowering output quality at all. Which TWO levers fit that constraint? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Moving every route to a smaller model tier.
options.explanation: A smaller model is a tradeoff that may lower quality. It needs an eval before it is applied.

options.text: Setting max_tokens below the typical response length.
options.explanation: This truncates answers and lowers quality. Truncated answers also tend to be retried, which costs more.

options.text: Lowering effort on every route.
options.explanation: Lower effort trades thoroughness for cost, which risks quality on hard tasks.

options.text: Prompt caching for the large, stable prefix that every request repeats.
options.explanation: Correct. Caching charges much less for repeated input and doesn't change what the model sees or produces.

options.text: The Message Batches API for the workloads nobody waits on, such as nightly reports and evals.
options.explanation: Correct. Batch processing halves token prices while running the same model and prompt.

stem: A fantasy-league assistant runs on many worker processes. Each worker builds its tools list from a plugin registry whose iteration order differs between processes. The 20,000-token system prompt is cached, but cache_read_input_tokens stays near zero whenever a request lands on a different worker than the one before. Which fix best fits?

options.text: Move the cache breakpoint onto the user message so the tools are no longer part of the prefix.
options.explanation: Tools render before the system prompt and messages, so they are in the prefix wherever the breakpoint sits. A changing tool order still breaks the match.

options.text: Switch to the 1-hour cache duration so that each separate worker keeps its own cached entry for longer.
options.explanation: A longer TTL doesn't make different prefixes match. Each tool order would still need its own cache write.

options.text: Serialize the tools in a fixed order, such as sorted by name, so every worker sends identical bytes.
options.explanation: Correct. Caching is an exact prefix match, and tools come first in that prefix. A deterministic tool order makes every request's prefix identical, so any worker can read the cached entry.

options.text: Place the tool definitions after the system prompt so that changes to them don't affect the cache.
options.explanation: The request renders tools first, then system, then messages, and the client can't change that order. The fix is to make the tool list stable.

stem: A draft-night assistant shares a 60,000-token cached prefix across all fans. After each deploy, the first fan's question is noticeably slower because the prefix must be written to the cache, and later questions are fast. The team wants that first real question to be fast too, at minimal cost. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Switch the shared prefix to the 1-hour cache duration so the entry survives each deploy.
options.explanation: A new deploy that starts cold still has to write the entry once, and a longer TTL costs more per write. It doesn't remove the first slow request.

options.text: On startup, send a max_tokens 0 request with the same prefix, model, thinking and effort settings.
options.explanation: Correct. A max_tokens 0 request writes the cache and returns without generating output, so the first real question reads from cache. The settings must match real traffic, or the warm-up writes an entry that traffic never hits.

options.text: On startup, send a short warm-up question at low effort so that it costs less than a real fan request.
options.explanation: Thinking and effort settings are part of what gets cached, so a warm-up with different settings may write an entry real traffic doesn't read. It also bills output tokens that nobody uses.

options.text: Remove caching from the first request after a deploy and only enable it from the second one on.
options.explanation: Without caching on the first request, nothing is written, so the second request becomes the slow one. The cold start just moves.

stem: A long coaching chat moves its cache breakpoint to the latest turn on every request, and cache reads normally cover the whole earlier conversation. Which two changes made mid-conversation would make the cached conversation history miss on the next request? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Appending the fan's new message after the previous turn
options.explanation: New content after the cached prefix is the normal case. The earlier conversation is still read from cache.

options.text: Sending some turns to a cheaper model to save money
options.explanation: Correct. Caches are model-scoped, so a turn on a different model can't read the entry the first model wrote. The whole prefix is written again.

options.text: Turning streaming on for the next request in the chat
options.explanation: Streaming is a transport option, not part of the cached prefix, so switching it doesn't affect cache reads.

options.text: Changing the top-level effort level between two turns
options.explanation: Correct. Thinking and effort settings are part of the cached prompt, and a top-level change invalidates the cached messages. Pin effort per route instead of varying it per turn.

options.text: Moving the breakpoint forward to the newest user turn
options.explanation: This is the recommended checkpointing pattern. Earlier breakpoints remain valid read points, so the history is still read from cache.
